extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in combinatorial and convex geometry; readers of 'Proofs from THE BOOK'.
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and constructive proofs in discrete and convex geometry, including constructions and bounds for touching simplices, point-set angle problems, probabilistic constructions, and a polynomial/linear-algebra attack on Borsuk's conjecture counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound construction for f(d) ≥ 2^d (touching d‑simplices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a family of 2^d pairwise touching d-simplices in R^d together with a transversal line that hits the interior of every simplex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from a d-dimensional configuration with a transversal line; take two nearby parallel transversal lines so each simplex contains an orthogonal connecting interval (a 'ladder' of segments). Apply an affine coordinate transformation to place the ladder in a canonical rectangle R1 so that each simplex contains a segment S1(α) = {(α,x2,0,...,0)^T : −1 ≤ x2 ≤ 1} in its interior. Reflect this configuration to obtain a second family with segments S2(β) that intersect all S1(α). Embed into R^{d+1} by taking convex hulls conv(P ∪ {±e_{d+1}}) to build (d+1)-simplices touching pairwise; tilt the antidiagonal slightly to obtain a transversal line L_ε that meets every simplex. The proof proceeds by induction on dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perles' upper bound via B‑matrix counting (f(d) < 2^{d+1})
rubrics_metrics.description: Given r touching d-simplices, enumerate facet hyperplanes H_j, choose positive sides H_j^+, construct an r×s matrix B with entries in {+1,−1,0}, and derive a counting contradiction to bound r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define Bij = +1 if P_i has a facet in H_j and P_i ⊆ H_j^+, −1 if in the negative side, 0 otherwise. Each row has exactly d+1 nonzero entries. Replace zeros by all ±1 choices to form matrix C; since each original row yields 2^{s−d−1} distinct rows and all rows of C are distinct but there are only 2^s possible ±1 vectors, conclude 2^{s−d−1} r ≤ 2^s, hence r ≤ 2^{d+1}, and with an extra argument obtain strict inequality r < 2^{d+1}. Use existence of a point x not on any H_j and not in any P_i to show not all ±1-vectors occur in C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalences linking non‑obtuse angle sets, strips, and touching translates
rubrics_metrics.description: Several characterizations of point sets S ⊆ R^d with no obtuse angles: (i) for any pair si,sj there exists a strip (two parallel hyperplanes) containing S with si,sj on the boundary; (ii) translates P−si (for P = conv(S)) intersect in a common point but only touch; (iii) translates Q+si of some convex polytope touch pairwise; (iv) can replace Q by its Minkowski symmetrization Q* (centrally symmetric) preserving intersection and touching properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct Hij as the hyperplane through origin orthogonal to si−sj, then Hij+si and Hij+sj are parallel hyperplanes bounding the strip. Use the translation correspondence: P ⊆ strip between Hij+si and Hij+sj iff P−si and P−sj lie in different halfspaces wrt Hij, which shows the touching/intersection correspondence. For preserving touching under symmetrization, use that Q* = { (x−y)/2 : x,y ∈ Q } and algebraic manipulations with vertices to show (Q+si)∩(Q+sj) ≠ ∅ iff (Q*+si)∩(Q*+sj) ≠ ∅ and similarly for touching (no intersection after small perturbation). These equivalences are used to relate combinatorial/metric questions to packing/volume arguments (scaling factor 1/2 gives volume arguments bounding |S| ≤ 2^d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic method for constructing large acute-angle 0/1 point sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomly select many 0/1 vectors in {0,1}^d, analyze 'bad triples' that create right angles via coordinate-wise conditions, bound expected number of bad triples, then delete a small set of vectors to obtain a large subset with only acute angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick 3m random independent 0/1 vectors; define a triple (i,j,k) as bad if for apex at j the scalar product (x(i)−x(j))·(x(k)−x(j)) = 0 (equivalently coordinate-wise equalities). Compute the probability a fixed triple is bad (product over coordinates, here (3/4)^d per coordinate analysis leads to overall probability), use linearity of expectation to bound expected number of bad triples (no independence needed), pick parameter m function of d so expected bad triples ≤ m, and then remove at most m points to leave 2m vectors with no bad triple (only acute angles). Markov's inequality and basic probabilistic tools are referenced in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk counterexample construction via polynomial and linear‑algebra methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct S ⊆ {±1}^d of many points whose diameter cannot be reduced by partitioning into few parts, by: choose Q ⊆ {±1}^n with parity constraint; map x ↦ xx^T to rank‑1 matrices R; take subdiagonal entries to get point set S; use integer-valued polynomials modulo p to bound sizes of nearly-orthogonal-free subsets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let q = p^m, n = 4q−2, and Q = {x ∈ {±1}^n : x1 = 1, number of −1 coordinates even}. Prove (x·y) ≡ −2 (mod 4) for x,y∈Q and define nearly-orthogonal when |x·y|=2. Define integer-valued polynomial P(z) = binomial-coefficient expression of degree q−2 and use divisibility by p to build Fy(x) that vanishes mod p on other points but not on y. After reduction (remove x1 and use x_i^2=1) obtain squarefree polynomials in n−1 variables of degree ≤ q−2 that are Q-linearly independent; count squarefree monomials to bound sizes of nearly-orthogonal-free subsets. Map to matrices M(x)=xx^T; show scalar products satisfy (M(x),M(y))=(x·y)^2 and minima correspond to nearly-orthogonal pairs; project to subdiagonal coordinate vectors U(x) to obtain S in R^{n(n−1)/2} whose maximal pairwise distance occurs exactly for nearly-orthogonal x,y. From these size bounds derive lower bounds g(q) on number of parts needed for diameter-reducing partitions, producing explicit counterexamples to Borsuk's conjecture in large dimension (e.g., q=9 yields d=561).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scalar‑product and matrix embeddings to compare distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed ±1-vectors x into rank-1 matrices xx^T and then into vectors of their subdiagonal entries to translate questions about angles/dot-products into Euclidean distances, allowing combinatorial extremal arguments about diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute (M(x),M(y)) = (x·y)^2; relate this to (U(x),U(y)) where U(x) collects subdiagonal entries: (M(x),M(y)) = 2(x·y_subdiag) + n, so inequalities on x·y translate to distance inequalities among U(x). Thus maximal Euclidean distance in the constructed point set corresponds exactly to nearly-orthogonal pairs; use this to translate combinatorial bounds into metric diameter bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: General constructive/proof techniques emphasized
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred proof techniques include affine coordinate transformations, reflections/ symmetrizations, induction on dimension, combinatorial counting by encoding configurations as ±1/0 matrices, probabilistic expectation arguments without independence assumptions, and number-theoretic polynomial divisibility arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly applies: affine maps to normalize configurations; reflections to produce symmetric/copied configurations; convex hulls to lift to higher dimensions; encoding combinatorial/geometric structure into matrices (B,C,xx^T) to enable counting arguments; linearity of expectation to bound expected number of undesirable structures; integer-valued polynomials and modular divisibility to rule out large independent sets. Each technique comes with a checklist of hypotheses (e.g., full-dimensionality, parity constraints, choice of prime power q) that must be satisfied for the method to apply.
